meta.title: Who really said "Lead, follow, or get out of the way"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Thomas Paine, not Iacocca. The motto is in American print by January 1961 as an unattributed motto; Iacocca used it in Chrysler's Jeep advertising.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Lead, follow, or get out of the way'?
meta.ogDescription: An anonymous motto documented in print from January 1961 — office desks by 1963, long before Ted Turner's desk, the 1981 book title, or Iacocca's Chrysler ads.

answer.label: Not Thomas Paine, not Lee Iacocca — an anonymous motto
answer.authorDates: In American print by 23 January 1961 · no author ever named
answer.sourceLine: Barry Popik’s citation file traces the saying in print to at least 1961, and the earliest item he lists — a Greensboro (NC) Daily News column of 23 January 1961 — already presents it as an anonymous motto someone had “saw this motto someplace,” with no author attached. Iacocca used the line in Chrysler’s Jeep advertising after Chrysler bought Jeep in 1987; he did not coin it, and no source ties the wording to him first.

source.excerpt: Carson Bain saw this motto someplace: “Lead. Follow. Or get out of the way!”
trail: Barry Popik’s Big Apple entry of 4 June 2010 states the phrase “has been cited in print since at least 1961 and was put on many office signs” ↗, and lists the Greensboro column of 23 January 1961 first.
The Thomas Paine Historical Association’s quotations FAQ says the line “does not exist in the Paine corpus, and seems to have its origin in the 20th century” ↗.
Wikiquote places it under the Misattributed heading on its Thomas Paine page ↗, pointing instead to Patton’s “Lead me, follow me, or get out of my way.”

MotorCities’ 10 July 2019 obituary piece by Robert Tate records the Iacocca connection as advertising: when he introduced the new Jeep, “the ad campaign advised to ‘Lead, Follow or Get Out of the Way!’” ↗.
source.excerptNote: The wording of the first known appearance is three sentences, not one, and the columnist attributes it to nobody — it is already a motto seen “someplace.” Popik’s file also records James A. Rhodes — later Ohio’s governor — using the same idea in his own words in the Bryan (OH) Times: “There’s three things you can do. You can lead, follow or get out of the way. I’m going to have to lead.” (Popik dates that item 19 March 1961, though the transcribed text calls Rhodes governor — an office he did not hold until January 1963.)

source.rightsNote: No rights status can honestly be asserted. The wording has no identifiable author and no identifiable first publication: it enters the record in a January 1961 newspaper column already unattributed, as a motto its subject had seen somewhere. Short proverbial phrases of this kind are generally not protectable on their own, but the individual newspaper articles, books and advertisements that carry it — including Christian Williams’ 1981 Ted Turner biography and Chrysler’s advertising copy — remain under their own copyrights.

author.name: Lee Iacocca
author.heading: The man the quote gets pinned on
author.metaLine: 1924–2019 · Ford and Chrysler executive; Chrysler chairman and CEO 1979–1992
author.bio: Lido Anthony “Lee” Iacocca was born in Allentown, Pennsylvania on 15 October 1924, rose to the presidency of Ford, was fired in 1978, and then ran Chrysler through the federal loan-guarantee rescue, the K-car and the minivan before retiring on 31 December 1992. He was his own pitchman — the man who said “If you can find a better car, buy it” on camera — which is exactly why stray leadership slogans stick to his name. He used “Lead, follow or get out of the way” in Chrysler’s Jeep advertising, but the motto was already circulating on American office desks long before he reached Chrysler.

copyAttribution: "Lead, follow, or get out of the way" — not Lee Iacocca, and not Thomas Paine. It is an anonymous American desk-sign motto, in print by 23 January 1961 (Greensboro Daily News), years before Iacocca used it in Chrysler's Jeep advertising. Earliest citations collected by Barry Popik, The Big Apple. Via Quotle.info

misattribution.heading: Four famous names, none of them the source
misattribution.intro: This line is credited to whoever the speaker most admires. All four of the usual candidates are downstream of a motto that was already anonymous office furniture in 1961.

items.why: The Thomas Paine Historical Association states plainly that the quote does not exist in the Paine corpus and seems to have its origin in the 20th century ↗. Wikiquote carries it in the Misattributed section of its Thomas Paine page ↗. Mitt Romney used it as Paine in his Florida primary victory speech on 31 January 2012; Yale Book of Quotations editor Fred Shapiro called the idea that Paine said it “extremely ridiculous” ↗, and biographer Craig Nelson said flatly that Paine never said it.

The variant “Lead me, follow me, or get out of my way” is pinned on Patton in quotation anthologies and on social media, but Barry Popik notes it surfacing on the alt.quotations newsgroup on 20 January 1994 and records that there is no evidence Patton ever said it ↗.

Iacocca genuinely used the line: MotorCities records that when he introduced the new Jeep — after Chrysler bought American Motors in 1987 — “the ad campaign advised to ‘Lead, Follow or Get Out of the Way!’” ↗. But the motto was in American newspapers from January 1961, when Iacocca was still a Ford executive, and no source shows him originating the wording.

Broadcasting reported in 1976 that one of Turner’s miniature desk billboards read “Either lead, follow or get out of the way,” and Christian Williams used the phrase as the title of his 1981 Turner biography ↗. Turner made it famous; he did not invent it either.

misattribution.truthLine: The honest answer is that nobody knows who first said it. It enters the record in January 1961 as an unsigned motto someone had simply seen somewhere, and was on office desks by 1963; every famous name attached to it since is a borrower — see Popik’s citation ladder ↗.

context.heading: Why this one travels
lead: This is a desk-plaque proverb, not a quotation. The early sightings collected by Barry Popik are exactly what office folklore looks like: a motto a Greensboro man had seen somewhere in January 1961; James A. Rhodes — Ohio’s auditor of state then, its governor from 1963 — telling reporters that “there’s three things you can do — you can lead, follow or get out of the way”; a sign on a Kansas businessman’s desk in 1963; a Rotary district governor in 1965; a home-economics banquet speech title in 1969. Nobody in that run is quoting anyone. They are all repeating something already in the air.

The famous names arrived afterwards and gave the line a fake pedigree. Broadcasting noted the motto on a miniature billboard on Ted Turner’s desk in 1976; Christian Williams took it as the title of his 1981 Turner biography; Chrysler’s Jeep advertising under Lee Iacocca put it on television; and in his Florida primary victory speech on 31 January 2012, Mitt Romney delivered it as Thomas Paine — a credit Paine scholars flatly reject.
detailsBody: 1961–1969 — anonymous. Greensboro (NC) Daily News, 23 Jan 1961 (“Lead. Follow. Or get out of the way!”); Bryan (OH) Times, dated 19 Mar 1961 by Popik (James A. Rhodes, Ohio’s governor from 1963); Dallas Morning News, 14 Mar 1963; Atchison (KS) Globe, 28 Jul 1963 (“a neat sign on a businessman’s desk”); Victoria (TX) Advocate, 18 Aug 1965; Lubbock Avalanche-Journal, 28 Mar 1969 — all in Popik’s file ↗.

1973–1981 — the celebrity phase. A sign in Battle Creek city manager Aaron Marsh’s office reported by The New York Times, 11 Dec 1973; Ted Turner’s desk billboard in Broadcasting (1976) and the St. Petersburg Times (1978); then Christian Williams’ biography Lead, follow or get out of the way: the story of Ted Turner ↗ (Times Books, 1981).
context.pull: It became famous as a sign on a desk, not a line in a book.

schema.claimQuoteText: Lead, follow, or get out of the way
schema.verdictNote: Commonly misattributed to Thomas Paine, and to George S. Patton in the variant wording “Lead me, follow me, or get out of my way.” The true author is not established; no creator is asserted here. Lee Iacocca did use the line in Chrysler’s Jeep advertising, but did not originate it.

sourcesVerified.claim: The saying has been cited in print since at least 1961; the earliest listed citation is the Greensboro (NC) Daily News, 23 January 1961, "Monday Moanin'" by W. Rhodes Weaver, p. B1 col. 5: "Carson Bain saw this motto someplace: 'Lead. Follow. Or get out of the way!'" The page also records an item it dates 19 March 1961, from the Bryan (OH) Times, quoting James A. Rhodes — the transcribed text calls him "Gov.", though Rhodes was Ohio auditor of state until his inauguration as governor on 14 January 1963, so the year is likely a typo for 1963 — an Atchison (KS) Globe businessman's desk sign of 28 July 1963, the New York Times of 11 December 1973, Ted Turner's desk billboard in Broadcasting v.90 (1976), and states there is no evidence Thomas Paine or George S. Patton ever said it. Entry dated 4 June 2010.

Wikiquote's Thomas Paine page lists "Lead, follow, or get out of the way." under the section heading "Misattributed", cross-referencing George S. Patton: "Lead me, follow me, or get out of my way", as quoted in Pocket Patriot: Quotes from American Heroes (2005) edited by Kelly Nickell, p. 157.
The Thomas Paine Historical Association states that "Lead, follow, or get out of the way" does not exist in the Paine corpus and seems to have its origin in the 20th century.

In his Florida primary victory speech on 31 January 2012 Mitt Romney attributed the line to Thomas Paine; Fred Shapiro, editor of the Yale Book of Quotations, called the notion that Paine said it "extremely ridiculous" and too modern in diction, and Paine biographer Craig Nelson said Paine never said it. Article dated 1 February 2012.
Christian Williams (b. 1943), Lead, follow or get out of the way: the story of Ted Turner, Times Books, New York, 1981 — the phrase used as a book title about Ted Turner.

Robert Tate's 10 July 2019 MotorCities article states that in 1987 Chrysler purchased American Motors from Renault, adding Jeep, and that "When Iacocca introduced the new Jeep, the ad campaign advised to 'Lead, Follow or Get Out of the Way!'" It also notes Iacocca retired from Chrysler in 1992 and died on 2 July at age 94.

Lee Iacocca was born 15 October 1924 in Allentown, Pennsylvania and died 2 July 2019; he was president of Ford until being fired in 1978, became Chrysler president in November 1978 and chairman and CEO in September 1979, and retired 31 December 1992. The article does not mention "lead, follow, or get out of the way"; his trademark advertising line was "If you can find a better car, buy it."
